division.heading: Actions Started by Statement of Claim

operative_text.controlling:
3.25   A statement of claim must
(a) be in Form 10,
(b) state the claim and the basis for it,
(c) state any specific remedy sought, and
(d) comply with the rules about pleadings in Part 13, Division
3.

BOOK_A.commentary:
Generally on the contents of pleadings, see R.13.6n. There are notices to the profession giving guidelines for email or digitally-filed documents, found in the "News and Announcements" part of the Court of King's Bench website.See R.3.8n.

Some documents can be submitted to the Court of King's Bench using its Filing Digital Service, but others only by email.The Court of King's Bench website lists accepted document types.There are strict naming conventions for documents filed by email. Among the palpable errors found to have been committed by a trial judge was deciding the case on a basis which was not in the pleadings.

A statement of claim is not a method of starting an arbitration, and should not be interpreted as doing so and thus stopping the limitation period from running, particularly if it does not talk about arbitration or ask for arbitration.A lawsuit and arbitration are conceptually distinct processes, virtually opposite of each other. BOOK_B.title: Contents of statement of claim

commentary.text: Rule 3.25 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.25. Remedies What is included, or not included, in the pleadings is important in terms of remedy. In Mazepa v. Embree, 2014 ABCA 438, 2014 CarswellAlta 2286, 588 A.R. 288, 14 Alta. L.R. (6th) 83, the Court said: 8 It is well-established that a trial or chambers judge should not decide a case on a matter not pleaded, and specifically should not grant remedies beyond the pleadings; the cases are noted in Sumner v PCL Constructors Inc., 2011 ABCA 326 at para. 26, 51 Alta LR (5th) 266, 515 AR 231; Dow Agrosciences Canada Inc. v Philom Bios Inc., 2007 ABCA 122, at paras. 60–2, 31 BLR (4th) 40, leave denied [2007] 3 SCR viii, and Paniccia Estate v Toal, 2012 ABCA 397 at para. 32, 71 Alta LR (5th) 411, 539 AR 349. The appellant particularly relies on statements to that effect in Wild Rose School Division No. 66 v Bert Pratch Const. Co., 1998 ABQB 831, 238 AR 339. Wild Rose was an action for the cost of constructing a school, which was brought after the school burned down. The Court made the general observation at para. 21 that the position of the parties is presumed to be set out in the pleadings, and said: “A court's jurisdiction to grant a remedy is limited by the pleadings of the party”. 9 While it is well-established that relief should be limited to what is pleaded, that rule is not absolute or truly “jurisdictional”: (a) First of all, the term “jurisdiction” has many meanings. In its very strictest sense, it refers to the court's ability to embark on the inquiry from the outset. However, it is often used to simply indicate in more general terms the boundaries of what can or should be done and not done. The limitation on the court's ability to grant the relief in Wild Rose was not jurisdictional in the strict sense. (b) Secondly, while the court is limited by the pleadings, the effect of the rule is reduced by the concurrent ability of the court to amend the pleadings at any time: R. 3.65. The Court in Wild Rose could have amended the pleadings, even during argument, if it was satisfied that there was no surprise or prejudice involved. The Court at all times had jurisdiction over the parties and the subject matter, and that jurisdiction (in the strict sense) was not limited or compromised by the scope of the pleadings. (c) Thirdly, procedural requirements (and any corresponding procedural irregularities) generally do not have any effect on the court's jurisdiction. Rule 1.5(1) states: 1.5. (1) If a person contravenes or does not comply with these rules, or if there is an irregularity in a commencement document, pleading, document, affidavit or prescribed form, a party may apply to the Court (a) to cure the contravention, non-compliance or irregularity, or (b) to set aside an act, application, proceeding or other thing because of prejudice to that party arising from the contravention, non-compliance or irregularity. Procedural shortcomings are considered to be “mere irregularities”, not jurisdictional in nature: Stout Estate v Golinowski Estate, 2002 ABCA 49 at paras. 76–82, 100 Alta LR (3d) 5, 299 AR 13. (d) Fourthly, relief can sometimes be granted on conditions. It is not necessary that the specific conditions be pleaded. Here the Court was only prepared to grant exclusive possession of the matrimonial home if alternative arrangements were made for the support of the respondent. Sections 68 and 69 of the Family Law Act, RSA 2000, c. F-4.5 specifically make support obligations relevant to exclusive possession applications. The resulting order does not violate the rule that the Court is limited to the pleadings. (e) Fifthly, the parties can always consent to matters of procedure, such as amendments to the pleadings, or the resolution of the case on issues not strictly pleaded. That consent can be express or implied. Here, previous counsel for the appellant explicitly advised the original chambers judge that the appellant would waive any shortcomings in the pleadings, and the absence of any affidavit evidence on the respondent's means and needs, and invited the Court to grant spousal support. Since the Court had, at all times, jurisdiction over the parties and the subject matter, there was no legal impediment to the Court giving effect to these parties' consent. It follows that it is not helpful to describe any procedural limitations identified here as “jurisdictional” in nature, and they do not render the order a “nullity”. In Wagner v. Wagner, 2014 ABCA 428, 2014 CarswellAlta 2262, 588 A.R. 218, 626 W.A.C. 218, the Court said: [27] Normally, a court should not give relief that a party has not […] expressly sought in the notice of application or pleading. Natural justice requires that the opposing party know what is being sought, and why. Usually that information is only available from the notice of application, although that is not always so. The opposing party may know what relief is sought, and why, by some other means and in enough time to marshal his or her arguments and evidence: DWH v DJR, 2013 ABCA 240 at paras 41–44, 556 AR 81. This is not to suggest that ferreting through affidavits for the issues to be decided is ideal. Relief sought should be stated with precision in a notice of application, and not left to be divined from other documents filed.

commentary.text:
Statements of claim must comply with this rule. However, if an improper form is used, or the claim is deficient in some way, rule 1.5 could save such non-convention or irregularity.
